name: Pūraṇa Kassapa
summary: One of the six famous teachers of the Pali canon, leader of an order. DN 2 reports his doctrine of non-action (akiriya): the one who kills, steals or lies does no evil, and gifts, self-control and truthfulness bring no merit. SN 22.60 and SN 46.56 ascribe to him the view that there is no cause for defilement, purification, knowing or not knowing; AN 6.57 ascribes to him the six classes of birth in which the Ājīvika leaders are 'supremely white'. In the Tamil Maṇimēkalai and Nīlakēci, Pūraṇa is the Ājīvika teacher. Buddhist legend (Dhammapada commentary, Divyāvadāna) says he drowned himself after the Buddha's Twin Miracle.

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (contemporary of the Buddha and Mahāvīra)

notes: All doctrine reported_by_opponent. The commentary's story that he was a slave named 'Full' (pūraṇa) because his birth completed a hundred slaves (Sumaṅgalavilāsinī) is recalled with low confidence.

name: Makkhali Gosāla
summary: Leader of the Ājīvikas. DN 2 reports his doctrine of purification through transmigration: there is no cause for the defilement or purification of beings, no human effort; all beings are shaped by destiny, circumstance and nature (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva) and, fool and wise alike, make an end of suffering after 8,400,000 great aeons, like a ball of string unwinding. AN 3.137 calls his doctrine the worst of all. The Jain Bhagavatī Sūtra (15) tells his birth in a cowshed, six years as Mahāvīra's companion, his claim to be a Jina, the confrontation at Sāvatthī, and his death in delirium followed by repentance; the Jain Isibhāsiyāiṃ (11) nevertheless records a saying of 'the arhat seer Maṅkhaliputta'.

tradition.text: (Jain) died at Sāvatthī sixteen years before Mahāvīra

realization_account.text: (Ājīvika claim, as reported by the Jains) Gosāla declared himself a Jina and the last tīrthaṅkara of this age; (Jain account) he confessed on his deathbed that he was Mahāvīra's disciple and not a Jina, and will attain liberation only after many births.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (reported by an opponent)

notes: The name: Jain sources derive 'Gosāla' from his birth in a cowshed (gośālā) and 'Maṅkhaliputta' from his father Maṅkhali, a maṅkha (picture-showman); Buddhaghosa derives 'Makkhali' from 'don't stumble' (mā khali) — both are the traditions' etymologies.

name: Ajita Kesakambalī
summary: One of the six famous teachers, named for his blanket of human hair. DN 2 reports his annihilationism: there is no gift, sacrifice or offering, no fruit of good and bad deeds, no this world or other world, no mother or father, no spontaneously born beings, no ascetic who has realized the other world; the person is made of the four great elements, which return to their masses at death, the faculties passing into space; fool and wise alike are annihilated at the body's breaking up.
alt_names: 阿夷陀翅舍欽婆羅 (Chinese, Dīrgha-āgama)

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (contemporary of the Buddha and Mahāvīra)

notes: Doctrine reported_by_opponent. Later tradition and scholars treat him as a forerunner of the Lokāyata; no text links him to that school by lineage. SN 44.9 reports (surprisingly) that he too declared where his dead disciples were reborn.

name: Pakudha Kaccāyana
summary: One of the six famous teachers. DN 2 reports his doctrine of seven bodies (kāya) — earth, water, fire, air, pleasure, pain and the soul — unmade, barren, firm as a pillar, unmoving, not affecting one another, so that one who cuts off a head with a sharp sword takes no life: the sword only passes through the space between the seven bodies.

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (contemporary of the Buddha and Mahāvīra)

notes: Doctrine reported_by_opponent. The Pali commentary's report that he avoided cold water is recalled with low confidence. His seven bodies reappear merged with niyati in Ja 545 and in the fourth 'negation' of MN 76.

name: Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta
summary: One of the six famous teachers, the type of the 'eel-wriggler'. DN 2 reports that asked whether there is another world, spontaneously born beings, fruit of deeds or a Tathāgata after death, he refused every alternative ('I do not say it is so, nor thus, nor otherwise, nor not so, nor not not so'); King Ajātasattu calls him the most foolish of the six. The Vinaya tells of the wanderer Sañjaya of Rājagaha, teacher of Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who left him with 250 wanderers for the Buddha, whereupon hot blood gushed from Sañjaya's mouth.

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (contemporary of the Buddha and Mahāvīra)

notes: The Vinaya (Mv 1.23) says only 'Sañjaya the wanderer'; the identification with Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta of DN 2 is the commentaries' and is questioned by some scholars. Do not confuse with tch:sanjaya (the Mahābhārata's narrator).

name: Mahāvīra
summary: U33 contribution: in the Pali canon he appears as Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta (Aggivessana), one of the six famous teachers; DN 2 reports his teaching as the 'fourfold restraint' (cātuyāma-saṃvara), a report that differs from the Jain canon's own account (five great vows; the fourfold restraint is Pārśva's, Uttarādhyayana 23). The Jain Bhagavatī Sūtra 15 makes him Gosāla's teacher and opponent.

name: Bṛhaspati
summary: U33 contribution: the Lokāyata is 'Bṛhaspati's doctrine'. The tradition's account makes him the preceptor of the gods who composed a deluding doctrine for the asuras (Maitrī Up. 7.9) and gave it to his disciple Cārvāka (Prabodhacandrodaya 2); the Bṛhaspati Sūtra, quoted as 'the venerable Bṛhaspati' by Jayarāśi, is ascribed to him, as are the anti-Vedic verses at the end of the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha's first chapter. The Arthaśāstra's 'Bārhaspatyas' (1.2.4) hold that only economics and government are sciences.
notes: Scholars distinguish the Lokāyata author (if a person) from the Vedic deity; recorded under the registry id per the tradition's identification.

name: Cārvāka (the eponymous teacher)
summary: The legendary disciple of Bṛhaspati after whom the school is named; in the Prabodhacandrodaya (Act 2) he is the servant of Great Delusion who spreads the Lokāyata through his pupils. Guṇaratna and others derive the name from 'chewing' (carv) — those who 'swallow' merit, demerit and the unseen — or from 'pleasing speech' (cāru-vāk).
notes: Distinct from tch:carvaka-raksasa of the Mahābhārata; the texts do not identify the two.

name: Cārvāka the rākṣasa (Mahābhārata)
summary: In MBh 12.39 a rākṣasa, friend of Duryodhana, who in the guise of a mendicant (a Sāṃkhya with tuft and triple staff) denounces Yudhiṣṭhira as a kinslayer before the assembled brāhmaṇas and is burnt by their 'hum'; Kṛṣṇa explains that he had won from Brahmā fearlessness from all beings except when he insulted brāhmaṇas. He teaches no doctrine; Duryodhana (9.63.38) calls him 'the wanderer skilled in speech'.
notes: Listed under lin:carvaka only because the school's name coincides; the epic makes no link.

name: Kambalāśvatara
summary: A Lokāyata author quoted by Śāntarakṣita: 'cognition arises from the body alone, sustained by the in- and out-breaths' (Tattvasaṅgraha 1864); Kamalaśīla calls this 'the sūtra: kāyād eva'.

name: Purandara (Cārvāka)
summary: A Cārvāka author quoted by Kamalaśīla: 'the Cārvākas too accept inference as known in the world; what is rejected is inference that some state by transgressing the worldly path' (Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā on 1481–82).
notes: Do not confuse with tch:purandara-dasa (the Kannada Haridāsa poet).

name: Aviddhakarṇa
summary: An author cited several times in Kamalaśīla's Pañjikā, including a 'Tattvaṭīkā'; later sources name him as a commentator on the Bṛhaspati Sūtra, while other passages show him arguing as a Naiyāyika. His affiliation is disputed.
notes: Kamalaśīla's citations checked locally (TSP lines on atoms, inference, the two means of knowledge); the Cārvāka affiliation is not confirmed by those passages.

name: Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa (Udbhaṭa)
summary: A commentator on the Bṛhaspati Sūtra known from citations in later Nyāya and Jain works, who is said to have reinterpreted the sūtras (e.g. allowing more than perception).
notes: Recalled from modern studies of the fragments (citations in Cakradhara's Granthibhaṅga and Vādideva's Syādvādaratnākara); not verified.

name: Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tattvopaplavasiṃha, the only complete surviving work of the Lokāyata current. He quotes 'the venerable Bṛhaspati' and argues that no definition of any means of knowledge can be made good, so that no principle — not even the four elements — can be established; worldly conduct proceeds without examination.

name: Nanda Vaccha
summary: Named with Kisa Saṅkicca and Makkhali Gosāla as one of the three Ājīvika leaders: 'supremely white' in Pūraṇa's six classes (AN 6.57), the only three the Ājīvikas recognize as having made an end (MN 76), and models of bodily austerity (MN 36).

name: Kisa Saṅkicca
summary: The second of the three Ājīvika leaders named in AN 6.57, MN 36 and MN 76.

name: Upaka the Ājīvaka
summary: The first person the newly awakened Buddha met on the road from Gayā; told of the Buddha's awakening he said 'may it be so' and went another way (MN 26; Vinaya Mv 1.6). The Therīgāthā verses of Cāpā tell of her husband Kāḷa, formerly an ascetic with a staff, who left her to go forth; the commentary identifies him with Upaka.

name: Hālāhalā
summary: A woman potter of Sāvatthī, lay follower of the Ājīvikas, in whose pottery-hall Gosāla lived and died (Bhagavatī Sūtra 15).

name: Saddālaputta
summary: A wealthy Ājīvika potter of Polāsapura, lay follower of Gosāla, who became a follower of Mahāvīra after being asked who makes his pots (Uvāsagadasāo 7).

name: Ayampula
summary: An Ājīvika lay follower of Sāvatthī who, in Bhagavatī 15, comes to ask the dying Gosāla a question and is answered in his delirium.

name: Guṇa Kassapa (Jātaka)
summary: A naked ascetic (acela) of the Kassapa clan in the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka whose doctrine combines fatalism, Pakudha's seven bodies and purification through 84 great aeons; the text does not call him an Ājīvika, but the doctrine is the Ājīvika one of DN 2.

name: Pāyāsi
summary: A chieftain (rājañña) of Setavyā in Kosala who held that there is no other world, no spontaneously born beings and no fruit of deeds, and tested it on condemned criminals; converted by Kumāra Kassapa, he was reborn as a minor deity (DN 23).
notes: Listed under lin:carvaka as a holder of the materialist view in a Buddhist narrative; the text gives no school name.

name: Paesi (Pradeśin)
summary: King of Seyaviyā in the Jain Rājapraśnīya who held that soul and body are the same and tested it on criminals; converted by the monk Kesi, poisoned by his queen, reborn as the god Sūriyābha.

name: Kesi Kumāra (Keśi)
summary: U33 contribution: a monk of Pārśva's line who converts King Paesi (Rājapraśnīya) and who, in Uttarādhyayana 23, meets Mahāvīra's disciple Goyama and agrees that the fourfold restraint and the five vows have one aim.

name: Kumāra Kassapa
summary: U33 contribution: the monk who refutes Pāyāsi's materialism with fourteen similes (DN 23).

name: Śīlāṅka
summary: U33 contribution: Śvetāmbara commentator on the Ācārāṅga and Sūtrakṛtāṅga, whose commentary derives the 363 rival views and explains the ajñānika maxim 'ignorance is better'.

name: Guṇaratna
summary: U33 contribution: author of the Tarkarahasyadīpikā on Haribhadra's Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, a main Jain report on the Lokāyata.

name: Aśoka (Piyadasi)
summary: U33 contribution: Maurya emperor whose edicts pair brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas, urge honour to all sects, name the Ājīvikas among the orders cared for, and who dedicated caves in the Barābar hills to the Ājīvikas. Buddhist legend (Divyāvadāna) also says an Ājīvika at his father's court foretold his kingship.
